record.paper_title: Open Problems Related to Quantum Query Complexity
record.context_brief: Query-space tradeoffs for collision and element distinctness
record.original_question: For the collision problem and the element distinctness problem, what are the optimal tradeoffs between the number of quantum queries and the amount of memory used? In the collision problem, a black-box function f:{1,...,n}->{1,...,m}, with n even and m at least n, is promised to be either one-to-one or two-to-one and the task is to decide which. In the element distinctness problem, a black-box function f:{1,...,n}->{1,...,m} is given with no promise and the task is to decide whether f is one-to-one. The tradeoff should account for the number of qubits, classical bits, or coherently queryable classical bits (qRAM) available to the quantum algorithm.

evidence.quote: In the collision problem, we’re given black-box access to a function f :{1, . . . , n}→{ 1, . . . , m} (where n is even and m≥ n), and are asked to decide whether f is 1-to-1 or 2-to-1, promised that one of those is the case. In the element distinctness problem, we’re given black-box access to a function f :{1, . . . , n}→{ 1, . . . , m}, with no promise, and are simply asked whether f is 1-to-1.

Problem 3 What are the optimal tradeoffs between the number of queries used by a quantum algorithm to solve the collision or the element distinctness problems, and the number of qubits or classical bits of memory?

For element distinctness, even supposing that we need a large memory, it would also be interesting to know whether the memory needs to be made of qubits, or whether coherently-queryable classical bits (a so-called “qRAM”) would suffice.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider two black-box problems on functions f : {1,...,n} → {1,...,m}, accessed via a quantum oracle that performs |x,y⟩ ↦ |x, y ⊕ f(x)⟩.

(a) Collision problem: n is even, m ≥ n, and f is promised to be either one-to-one or exactly two-to-one. Decide which.

(b) Element distinctness problem: no promise is given on f; decide whether f is one-to-one.

A quantum algorithm for either task is characterized by three resources: T, the number of queries to the oracle; and a memory budget consisting of S_q "quantum" qubits (fully coherent workspace) together with possibly S_c "classical" bits or coherently-queryable classical bits (a "qRAM" of size S_c that can be addressed in superposition but whose contents are classical).

Determine the optimal tradeoff between T and the memory parameters (S_q, S_c) for bounded-error quantum algorithms solving the collision problem and the element distinctness problem. In particular:

(i) Establish matching upper and lower bounds on T as a function of (n, S_q, S_c) for each problem.

(ii) For element distinctness, decide whether large memory is in fact necessary, and if so, whether qRAM (coherently-queryable classical memory of size S_c with S_q = O(log n)) suffices to achieve the optimal query complexity, or whether genuine qubits of workspace are required.
artifact.status_search_result: The general quantum time–space tradeoff for element distinctness is explicitly stated as a long-standing open problem in recent work. Partial results exist: Hamoudi–Magniez (2021/2023) prove a T^3 S = Ω(K^3 N) tradeoff for finding K collision pairs in random functions, and there are matching upper bounds via quantum walks for certain regimes, but tight tradeoffs for the decision versions (collision and element distinctness), and the qubits-vs-qRAM question, remain unresolved.

status_evidence.title: Quantum Time-Space Tradeoff for Finding Multiple Collision Pairs
status_evidence.snippet: Any improvement to the current lower bound would imply a breakthrough for the Element Distinctness problem, which is a long-standing open question to prove a time-space lower bound for.
status_evidence.claim: Tight time-space lower bounds for element distinctness remain open.

status_evidence.title: Quantum Time–Space Tradeoff for Finding Multiple Collision Pairs (ACM ToCT)
status_evidence.snippet: Any quantum algorithm using S qubits of memory must perform T queries satisfying T^3 S = Ω(K^3 N) for finding K collision pairs.
status_evidence.claim: Only partial tradeoff results known, for the K-collision-pair variant.

status_evidence.title: Open Problems Related to Quantum Query Complexity
status_evidence.snippet: Problem 3 asks for the optimal tradeoffs between queries and memory for collision and element distinctness.
status_evidence.claim: The problem is posed as open.
